title: Tending the garden

cards: A plastic bag snagged on a fence by the bus stop, flapping in the wind. Everybody walks past it. It isn't anybody's bag, so it isn't anybody's job.
Now go back to the second chapter of the Bible. There's no city yet, no bus stop, no fence. There's a garden, and one human being, and before anything else goes wrong, God gives that human a job.
Not a title. Not a throne. A job, with dirt under the fingernails.

teach.b: Here's the verse, Genesis 2:15: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Two verbs.
Readers of the Hebrew point out that the first is a word for working the ground that elsewhere also means to serve.

The second, they note, means to keep, to guard, to watch over, and it's used for keeping God's commandments. So the human is placed in the garden as a gardener who serves it and a guard who protects it. Not an owner.
A psalm makes the ownership plain: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof."
Christians read the first chapter of Genesis too, where humans are given dominion over the creatures. Some readers once took dominion as permission to use things up.

Others, reading it beside chapter two, hear dominion as the responsibility of a steward: ruling the way a good king rules, for the good of what's in his care. Francis of Assisi sang of Brother Sun and Sister Water.
Leaders in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches have written about care for creation as part of faith, not a hobby beside it. It comes down to two old verbs: serve the ground, and guard it.

how: Christians practice creation care through church gardens, cleanups, energy and waste changes in congregations, and prayers for creation; some churches keep a Season of Creation each year, and Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant leaders have written on care for the earth.

o: keeping church grounds neat for worship
growing your own food at home, for health
caring for creation: serve it and guard it

games.q: the job in the garden — tap the pairs.
p: to dress it and to keep it

s: in Genesis 2, the human's job is to rule from a throne
the job is to dress the garden and keep it: work it and guard it.
the Bible's word for keep the garden is also used for keeping God's commandments
readers of the Hebrew note that the same word means to keep, guard and watch over.
Christians all read dominion the same way
some once took it as permission to use things up; others read it as a steward's responsibility.

games.q: you're the man God has just placed in the garden of Eden. what's the job?
o: dress it and keep it: work it and guard it.
games.why: Genesis 2:15: "to dress it and to keep it." before anything goes wrong, the human is given work: serving and guarding the ground.

practice: Picture a place you pass every day, a sidewalk, a parking lot, the hallway at work or school, and the bit of litter you always walk past there: a cup, a wrapper, a bag on a fence.
Picture yourself bending down to pick it up, not as a big gesture, but as the job given in the garden. If you pray, you can give thanks for that small patch of earth.

wordCard.voice: Tending the garden. Creation care, from Genesis 2:15: the human placed in Eden to dress it and keep it, to serve the earth and guard it.
